title: Higher-Order Components in Depth
body:
### How I think about it - An HOC is like passing a component through a piece of middleware: it takes a component, gives it something extra, and returns a new one. - That "something extra" can be data or UI. - For authorisation or data fetching, the parent does the work and passes the result down as props. - For error handling or extending the UI, the extra comes from wrapping more UI around the component on the way out. ```js function withExtraProp(Component) { return function(props) { return ; }; }}, []); ``` ### Details that matter - **An HOC does not modify the original component.** - It is a pure functional wrapper: it creates a new component (usually called the wrapper) and leaves the original alone. - This is the important rule. Mutating the original component's prototype would destroy its reusability. - **Naming** - HOCs are named `withSomething` (`withExtraProp`), so you can tell what it is at a glance. - You call it as `const EnhancedComponent = withSomething(MyComponent)`. - **Static methods get lost** - If the original component has statics (`defaultProps`, `fetchData`), wrapping drops them by default. Use `hoist-non-react-statics` to copy them across. - **Since React 18, HOCs are mostly for class components** - In function components, most HOC use cases are better served by a custom hook — shorter, and no extra layer in the tree. - Hooks have also filled out since React 18: `useSyncExternalStore`, `useId`, automatic batching, and so on. - A custom hook is excellent at sharing logic and data, but it cannot extend the UI. ### Where you use them - **Authorisation and permissions.** Some components should only be reachable by authenticated users. Write an HOC that takes a component and returns a new one that checks authentication before rendering. - **Data fetching.** The other common case. An HOC takes a component and returns one that fetches on mount and passes the data down as props. - **Error handling.** An HOC that wraps the original component's render and shows an error message or fallback when something throws. - **Purely extending the UI** — adding a layer around it. ### HOC vs custom hook | | Higher-order component | Custom hook | |---|---|---| | **Shape** | Takes a component → returns a new component | A `useXxx` function | | **Used for** | Sharing logic in class components, permissions, injecting data, wrapping UI | Sharing logic in function components, data fetching, state | | **Upsides** | - Works on class components
- Can change both UI and data | - Shorter, no extra nesting
- Better type inference | | **Downsides** | - Adds nesting (wrapper hell)
- Statics can be lost | - Cannot be used in class components
- Weak at extending UI | | **Cost** | One more component render | Essentially none | | **Statics** | Need `hoist-non-react-statics` | Not an issue | | **React 18 guidance** | For class components, or when you need to wrap UI | The default way to share logic between function components | | **Call site** | `withAuth(MyComponent)` | `const { data } = useAuth()` | ### In short - **Class component** ➜ use an HOC. - **Function component** ➜ custom hook when you are only sharing logic and data; HOC when you also need to wrap the markup. - **Both** ➜ an HOC can call a custom hook, but only inside the function component it returns. ```javascript function withAuth(Component) { // ❌ you cannot call useAuth() here return function Wrapper(props) { // ✅ but you can call hooks here const { user } = useAuth(); if (!user) return ; return ; }; } ``` ### What that mixed case tells you about hooks and HOCs - A custom hook cannot wrap UI, because **a hook is just a function: it returns data or methods**, and **it cannot return new JSX wrapped around your component**. - The rules of hooks: **hooks may only be called inside a function component or another custom hook**, never in an ordinary function or a class component. - An HOC is itself an ordinary function, so a hook cannot go at its top level. But what an HOC returns *is* a function component, so hooks are fine inside that.
